the isotopic signatures of fluvial sediments from the Darling sub-basins of the Murray Darling Basin (Australia) are similar to those of aeolian material from Antarctic ice cores.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the transport of aeolian dust from the Australian continent, which may have a significant impact on the Southern Ocean.
the potential impact of Australian dust in the Southern Ocean.
the transport and deposition of Australian dust to Antarctica, which has been poorly understood in the past, and the potential impact of this dust on the Antarctic environment and climate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Australian aeolian dust has a significant influence in the Southern Ocean, which in turn has a profound effect on climate and the global carbon cycle.
Australian aeolian dust has been deposited in Antarctica and in the Southern Ocean during the last 170 kyrs, and that this has occurred during interglacials.
the Southern Ocean would receive aeolian dust from the Australian continent, and in particular southeastern Australia, during interglacial and interstadial periods.

during wet periods in Australia (i.e. interglacial periods), the Australian dust plume would have been transported over the Southern Ocean, and deposited as dust on the ice sheets of West Antarctica.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the Australian source of aeolia dust to Antarctica is not restricted to the present day.
aeolian dust originating in southeastern Australia can be transported to Antarctica and the Southern Ocean and that this dust may play a role in the climate system.
